title: Certifying bipartite entanglement on a superconducting processor from a corrected QAOA cost layer
abstract: The Quantum Approximate Optimisation Algorithm is the canonical near-term heuristic, yet on real superconducting hardware its behaviour is set by device physics, not by the algorithm. Hardware demonstrations rarely prove the intended coupling is realised, that genuine entanglement is prepared, or what controls it. We report a pre-registered single-device study on the nine-qubit superconducting processor Red at the Barcelona Supercomputing Center, using its five-qubit component. Across six calibrations we certify bipartite entanglement of a corrected QAOA cost layer on the good coupler at depth one by two-qubit tomographic negativity: 0.077, BCa 95% CI [0.065, 0.091], excluding zero every day, while the coupling-off twin stays separable and the degraded coupler equals zero. We then measure the device physics directly: in a pre-registered manipulation on a fixed Bell preparation (not the QAOA layer), reducing the CZ pulse amplitude causally reduces the certified negativity along a positive, well-fit slope (R^2 = 0.83-0.96), every rung-level interval excluding zero and surviving Holm and Benjamini-Hochberg correction. This is a local linearisation of a peaked response, not a global monotone law: the negativity peaks at conditional phase |zeta| = pi, which the nominal amplitude overshoots. The J=0 twin is a separate off-state control and the fringe visibility is constant, so the effect is coherent. The average gate fidelity is non-monotone in the drive and is reported only as a diagnostic. A per-circuit statevector guardrail excludes a diagonal compilation fault we disclose and repair. A randomized-measurement witness is consistent with entanglement but underpowered. The certificate collapses by depth three, and a pre-registered sixteen-instance depth-three ensemble shows no optimisation signal (one-sided Wilcoxon p = 0.15). We claim no advantage; the instances are classically trivial.
summary: This paper rigorously certifies bipartite entanglement on a superconducting processor using the QAOA cost layer. The key achievement is demonstrating a measurable, causal relationship: deliberately reducing the CZ pulse amplitude predictably reduces the certified entanglement. This provides a deep, physics-grounded characterization of device performance rather than just algorithmic success.
main_problem: To move beyond simply reporting success against a random floor in hardware demonstrations of algorithms like QAOA, by rigorously certifying the physical entanglement generated by the device.
main_result: Bipartite entanglement was certified on the good coupler at depth one, and a causal dose-response law was established showing that reducing the CZ pulse amplitude causally reduces the certified negativity.
method: The study used two-qubit tomographic negativity to certify entanglement and performed pre-registered manipulations varying the CZ pulse amplitude to establish a causal relationship with the measured entanglement.
model_or_system: The experiment was conducted on a nine-qubit superconducting processor named "Red" at the Barcelona Supercomputing Center, focusing on the corrected QAOA cost layer implemented on a five-qubit component.
key_observables: Two-qubit tomographic negativity, CZ pulse amplitude, average gate fidelity, and the depth of the QAOA circuit.
important_parameters: Depth one (for entanglement certification), the CZ pulse amplitude (the control variable), and the resulting linear fit slope ($R^2 = 0.83-0.96$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on pre-registration for rigor; the authors explicitly claim no quantum advantage as the tested instances are classically solvable.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the connectivity of the superconducting processor, the reconstructed two-qubit density matrix showing coherences, and tables present the statistically derived dose-response slopes for certified negativity versus manipulated CZ pulse amplitude.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical system and the goal of rigorous entanglement certification. It presents the entanglement measurements, followed by the core experimental work: varying the CZ pulse amplitude to map out a causal, measurable relationship between device control and quantum resource (negativity). Finally, it discusses the limitations, depth collapse, and statistical robustness of the findings.
why_interesting: This work provides a highly detailed, quantitative characterization of entanglement generation on a real superconducting chip, moving beyond simple 'yes/no' demonstrations to map out the physical control landscape of quantum resources.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

figures.caption: Figure 1: Entanglement is certified on the good coupler at depth one and nowhere else. (a) Per-arm two-qubit reduced-state negativity from tomography, day-level mean with 95% confidence interval over six calibrations: the good edge 4-5 at p = 1 certifies (cold and warm), while the p = 3 arm, the coupling-off J = 0 twin and the degraded 6-8 edge are separable. (b) The independent randomized-measurement p3-PPT witness W = p2 2 −p3 on the good edge on a later calibration: W = 0.0105 with BCa 95% CI, clear of the Werner PPT-boundary null but — at this magnitude — underpowered against a near-pure-separable null, so reported as consistent with entanglement.

Figure 2: Reducing the manipulated CZ drive amplitude reduces the certified negativity along a positive, well-fit slope over the probed ladder. Certified two-qubit negativity (PSD, BCa) against the manipulated CZ pulse amplitude factor (the single knob we set), for three couplers of component B (4-5, 5-7, 6-8), two calibration sessions each (filled circles, session 1; open triangles, session 2). Lines are the per-edge weighted fits over the rung window; the legend gives the per-edge slope in certified negativity per unit fractional amplitude. Figure 3: The certificate collapses by depth three on b08; separately, the depth-three ensemble shows no optimisation signal. Left: the good-edge negativity present at p = 1 is separable by p = 3 (instance b08, day- level over six calibrations) — a within-instance depth collapse. Right: across the N = 16 ensemble measured at p = 3 only, per-instance optimum mass Popt sits at the uniform (1/32) and device-marginal Bernoulli floors (one-sided Wilcoxon versus Bernoulli p = 0.15, not significant); this speaks to p = 3 alone and is not evidence of a decline with depth.

Figure 4: The good coupler certifies on every calibration; the degraded coupler never does. Raw two-qubit negativity of the good edge 4-5 (upper) and the degraded edge 6-8 (lower) across the six daily calibrations, with the good-edge grand-mean band. Good above bad on 6/6 days; the separation is reported through the two per-edge day-level intervals (good BCa CI [0.065, 0.091], degraded TOST-equivalent to zero), because the pre-registered paired test is a secondary hypothesis that does not survive multiplicity correction (see text). Between-day standard deviation 0.016.

Figure 5: Component B of Red and its couplers. The calibrated connectivity read live from the runcard on 4 August 2026: nine qubits, seven CZ couplers, and the absent 3-4 bridge that splits the chip into components A = {0, 1, 2, 3} and B = {4, 5, 6, 7, 8}. Component B carries the primary instance b08, the good edge 4-5, the degraded edge 6-8 and the 5-7 coupler used in the causal experiment.
